name: Sophora flavescens (kushen)
short: 83 Sophora alkaloid poisonings by mouth (mostly kushen, often overdose): dizziness, vomiting; long QT in 1 also on ciprofloxacin. Liver harm: animal, lab, isolated cases. Matrine review: nerve harm.
text: A retrospective study of 83 laboratory-confirmed cases of acute poisoning with Sophora alkaloids taken by mouth, reported to the Hong Kong Poison Control Centre from 2008 to 2021 found Sophora flavescens to be the main source (77.1%), with an excessive dose common (39.0%); most patients (90.4%) had minor effects, mainly dizziness (83.1%), vomiting (72.3%) and palpitations (32.5%), and one patient needed close cardiac monitoring for a prolonged QT interval after also taking ciprofloxacin; ciprofloxacin is the only medicine the cited sources describe as taken together with Sophora, and the abstract does not say whether the two interacted. No acute liver or kidney injury or skin reactions were seen in the series; the authors contrast the absence of skin reactions after oral use with intravenous use of the herb, and note that liver toxicity has been reported in laboratory and animal studies and in isolated human case reports. In rats, a Sophora flavescens extract given by mouth for 14 days impaired liver function and caused fat to build up in the liver, and a mouse and laboratory study identified a Sophora flavescens component, isoxanthohumol, as a possible risk factor for liver injury, citing reports that the herb and its preparations may cause liver damage. A review of matrine, an alkaloid found in Chinese herbs such as Sophora flavescens and Radix Sophorae tonkinensis, states that an increasing number of published studies indicate serious adverse effects, most obviously liver toxicity and neurotoxicity; the abstract does not say whether these studies were in people, animals or the laboratory. In trials of kushen-based traditional Chinese medicine formulations for ulcerative colitis (8 trials, 983 participants; the abstract does not list the formulations' other ingredients), adverse events were less frequent than with 5-aminosalicylic acid, but the difference was not statistically significant (p = 0.06).
